g11-geography-ug5-t1.overview: Geographic location conditions the pace and pattern of development across agriculture, industry, settlements and services in every country. This lesson separates economic growth from development, weighs determinism against possibilism, and applies three classic location models to real spaces and markets.
objectives: Define economic growth and economic development and explain how development is measured
Contrast geographic determinism and possibilism as schools of thought on development
Explain how von Thunen's model orders agricultural land use concentrically around a market city
Apply Weber's least-cost reasoning and the material index to the siting of industries
Describe Christaller's central place hierarchy and its marketing, transportation and administrative principles
g11-geography-ug5-t1.simple: Economic growth is the quantitative increase in goods, services and GDP of a nation over a period, while economic development is the sustained, qualitative and quantitative improvement of people's material well-being. Development is measured with the Human Development Index, built from life expectancy, knowledge and real per capita income on a 0 to 1 scale. Two philosophies link location to development: determinism claims the geographic environment alone decides how countries develop, while possibilism argues that humans, using technology, can widen the possibilities the environment offers. Location theory then explains where activities sit. Von Thunen arranged farming in rings around a market city, Weber located industry where transport costs are least, and Christaller arranged settlements and service centers in a hexagonal hierarchy. Ethiopia scored 0.485 on the 2019 HDI, ranking 173 of 189 countries.
g11-geography-ug5-t1.detailed:
Growth versus development. Economic growth is an increase in goods and services, or growth of the gross domestic product (GDP), of a nation over a specific period; it focuses only on the quantitative growth of national per capita income, without regard to standards of living and welfare. Economic development is the sustained development of the material well-being of society, and it is both quantitative and qualitative: people become more educated and healthier, with good access to quality housing, better sanitation and employment opportunities. Development is often measured with the Human Development Index (HDI), a quantitative measure of well-being computed from three dimensions: longevity (long and healthy life, measured by life expectancy at birth), access to knowledge (literacy rates and average years of schooling among adults) and a decent standard of living (real per capita income). Each computed variable is first converted to a 0-1 scale and the scaled values are then added, so HDI values lie between 0 and 1. In the 2019 UNDP ranking of 189 countries, Norway led with 0.957, followed by Ireland and Switzerland (both 0.955), while Niger (0.394), the Central African Republic (0.397) and Chad (0.398) were at the bottom. Ethiopia scored 0.485 and ranked 173 of the 189 countries.

Determinism versus possibilism. Two contrasting philosophies link geography and development. Geographic determinism assumes that the stage of socio-economic development of countries is exclusively determined by their geographic environment - location, climate and landforms - and its theorists argued that temperate countries are more developed than tropical ones precisely because of these contrasting environments. This thinking began in the 15th century AD and persisted until the 1950s; its earliest adherents were Greek and Roman scholars such as Aristotle, Hippocrates and Strabo, and its leading modern advocates were Karl Ritter (1779-1859), Ellen Churchill Semple (1863-1932) and Elsworth Huntington (1876-1947). Possibilism replies that the environment is not the only determinant: development results from the interaction of geographic location and human factors, because the creative mind can modify environmental conditions into usable opportunities with the latest technologies. Its leading proponents were Lucien Paul Victor Febvre (1878-1956) and Paul Vidal de la Blache (1845-1918), whose well-known claims were that 'nature is never more than an adviser' and 'there are no necessities but everywhere possibilities'. Possibilism is now widely accepted, yet it does not mean location plays no role at all.

How location reaches the economy. Location is an integral part of economic geography, regional science and spatial economics, and it strongly influences the scope of firms situated in a place by controlling the distribution of the population (purchasing power), economic patterns, transport costs and trading networks. The cost of moving goods and services across spatial scales shapes the access of firms to markets, while transport costs and networks affect the relative relevance of firms and decisions about innovation and capital investment. Three classic theories examine what economic activities are located where and why - one for agriculture, one for industry, and one for settlements and service centers.

Von Thunen's agricultural rings. Johann Heinrich von Thunen (1783-1850), a German farmer and amateur economist, published his agricultural land-use theory in 1826 in the book The Isolated State. He imagined a single central market city standing at the heart of a plain of thorough physical similarity - an isotropic, self-sufficient 'Isolated State' with no external influence - and farmers who were equally rational everywhere. Land uses then arrange in concentric rings: perishable and heavy products (vegetables, fruit and dairy) are produced nearest the city; bulky forest products such as firewood and timber cover the second ring, because moving them farther would cost too much; field crops such as grains come from the third ring, since they cost relatively less to transport; ranching occupies the fourth ring, because animals can transport themselves to market; and beyond the fourth ring the land remains unoccupied wilderness. In the model, production costs stay the same as distance grows, transport costs increase, and locational rent decreases - transport cost and locational rent are inversely related. Land closest to the city costs more, which is still true today, although the isolated self-sufficient state and isotropic surface are unlikely to be found in reality.

Weber's least-cost industry. Alfred Weber (1868-1958), a professor of economics at the University of Heidelberg from 1907 to 1933, presented his least-cost industrial location theory in 1909 in Theory of the Location of Industries, later translated into English in 1929; it is considered the basis of modern industrial location theory. Weber assumed firms choose locations to minimize total costs and maximize profits within an isolated, isotropic region of perfect competition and complete market knowledge, with ubiquitous resources (water, air, sunlight, sand) and localized materials (labor, fuel, minerals, crops, wood). He identified three key factors - transport costs, labor costs and agglomeration economies - and treated transportation as the most important, adjusted for the other two, using a Location Triangle linking market, factory and input sources. He distinguished weight-losing inputs from weight-gaining ones and proposed the material index, the weight of inputs divided by the weight of outputs. If the material index is greater than 1, the firm should locate nearer the raw material source; if it is below 1, nearer the market. Cotton textiles, soft-drink bottling, breweries and wool processing can therefore sit near markets, while bauxite and iron-ore refineries and steel and sugar-cane mills - whose bulky inputs lose weight in processing - should locate near input sources. Industries using ubiquitous raw materials such as water and solar power are likely located closer to markets.

Christaller's central places. Walter Christaller (1893-1969), a German geographer, developed his central place theory in 1933 from a study of settlement patterns in southern Germany, asking how urban settlements are spaced and how goods and services are exchanged between orders of settlements. He assumed an isotropic, boundless plain, uniformly settled and equally served by transport, with equal incomes (purchasing power), rational consumers and producers, and perfect competition with no excessive profit. His model rests on three concepts: centrality, the pull of a particular center; the threshold, the minimum purchasing power (population and income) required to attract a firm or service provider; and the range, the maximum distance people travel to acquire goods and services. Because overlapping circles waste space, he drew a geometric hexagonal hierarchy with a large city, fewer towns, and many villages and hamlets, built on three principles: the marketing principle (K = 3), where 1, 3, 9, 27 ... centers are served so that many consumers obtain goods from few service centers; the transportation principle (K = 4), where lower-order settlements sit at the midpoints of the sides of the hexagons, cutting travel distance; and the administrative principle (K = 7), where six lower-order settlements are wholly served and controlled by the central place, matching political and social administration.

Shared strengths and limits. All three theories rest on an isotropic surface, equal purchasing power and a self-sufficient isolated state, assumptions rarely met in reality; von Thunen wrote before motor transport, refrigerators and railroads, and Weber focused on heavy industry while neglecting light industry and relief features. Yet the models remain cutting-edge tools: land rent still rises toward city centers, firms still balance input weights against market access, and planners still think in hierarchical levels of service provision.

keyTerms.def: An increase in the goods, services and gross domestic product of a nation over a specific period; a purely quantitative measure focused on per capita income.
The sustained development of the material well-being of society; qualitative and quantitative progress in education, health, housing, sanitation and employment.
A composite index between 0 and 1 built from life expectancy at birth, access to knowledge, and a decent standard of living measured by real per capita income.

The philosophy that socio-economic development is exclusively determined by the geographic environment of location, climate and landforms; advocated by Ritter, Semple and Huntington from the 15th century until about 1950.
The philosophy that development results from the interaction of location and human factors, because people can modify the environment into opportunities; championed by Febvre and Vidal de la Blache.
Weber's ratio of the weight of inputs to the weight of outputs; a value above 1 pulls the firm toward raw material sources, a value below 1 pulls it toward the market.
The return earned by land in von Thunen's model; it decreases as distance from the market city increases, in inverse relation to transport cost.
A settlement or nodal point that serves the surrounding area with goods and services, obeying Christaller's concepts of centrality, threshold and range.

workedExamples.problem: Compute the gap between the highest and lowest HDI scores in the 2019 UNDP ranking, and state what it implies about geographic patterns of development.
workedExamples.given: Norway scored 0.957 (rank 1) and Niger scored 0.394 in the 2019 ranking of 189 countries.
workedExamples.formula: HDI gap = highest HDI score - lowest HDI score
workedExamples.answer: The gap is 0.563 of a maximum of 1.0, showing that European states at the top and tropical African states at the bottom sit far apart on human well-being, the very pattern the determinist and possibilist debates try to explain.

workedExamples.problem: A sugar mill processes 10,000 tonnes of sugar cane into 1,000 tonnes of sugar per year. Using Weber's material index, decide where the mill should be located.
workedExamples.given: Weight of inputs (sugar cane) = 10,000 tonnes; weight of output (sugar) = 1,000 tonnes.
workedExamples.formula: Material index = weight of inputs / weight of outputs
workedExamples.answer: The material index is 10, well above 1, so the industry is bulk-reducing: the mill should locate nearer to the cane fields, like the sugar-cane mills Weber described.

workedExamples.problem: A soft-drink bottling plant mixes 300 kg of concentrate with 2,700 kg of common water to make 3,000 kg of bottled drinks. Where should the plant build?
workedExamples.given: Localized input (concentrate) = 300 kg; ubiquitous input (water) = 2,700 kg; output = 3,000 kg.
workedExamples.formula: Material index = weight of inputs / weight of outputs
workedExamples.calculation: Material index = 1, so treated through the ubiquitous resource logic the localized share is 300 / 3,000 = 0.1, far below 1.
workedExamples.answer: The product gains bulk while being made, so the plant should locate nearer the market, exactly as Weber grouped soft-drink bottling among industries located near consumers.

workedExamples.problem: Under Christaller's marketing principle, count how many lower-order centers of successive levels are served by one first-order (highest) central place, down to the third level.
workedExamples.given: Marketing principle K = 3, giving the serving sequence 1, 3, 9, 27 ...
workedExamples.formula: Number of centers at level n = 3 to the power of (n - 1)
workedExamples.calculation: Level 2 = 3 centers; level 3 = 9 centers; total lower-order centers = 12
workedExamples.answer: One top central place serves 3 second-order centers and 9 third-order centers (12 in all), which is why the K = 3 system serves many consumers from a few service centers.

commonMistakes: Treating economic growth and economic development as the same thing, when growth is only quantitative while development adds welfare and quality of life.
Swapping the champions of the two schools, for example crediting Febvre with determinism instead of possibilism.
Assuming determinism is still the accepted view, when possibilism is now widely accepted by geographers.
Forgetting that transport cost and locational rent move in opposite directions in von Thunen's model.
Reversing the material index rule, sending weight-losing industries such as sugar mills to markets instead of raw material sources.
Placing ranching in the inner rings, when ranching occupies the fourth ring because livestock are self-transporting.
Confusing the K systems, for example attaching K = 3 to the administrative principle rather than the marketing principle.
applications: Explaining Ethiopia's 2019 HDI of 0.485 (rank 173 of 189) as a combined schooling, health and income gap rather than a single cause.
Using von Thunen's rings to justify market gardens and dairying near Addis Ababa and grain farms farther out along the highways.
Applying Weber's material index to argue that Ethiopian sugar mills belong near cane plantations and breweries near city markets.
Using Christaller's threshold and range to decide which woreda towns justify hospitals, high schools or weekly markets.
Making the possibilist case that irrigation, drainage and upgraded transport can turn location limitations such as poor soils and remoteness into opportunities.
Reading any district map to identify which settlement could serve as the central place for its surrounding villages.
g11-geography-ug5-t1.summary: Economic growth measures the quantitative rise of income and output, while development adds qualitative well-being and is scored by the Human Development Index between 0 and 1 - Norway topped the 2019 ranking at 0.957 while Ethiopia ranked 173 with 0.485. Determinism credits the environment alone, but possibilism, now widely accepted, stresses human adjustment through technology. Von Thunen, Weber and Christaller each modelled how location orders agriculture, industry, and settlements and services around cost, distance and hierarchy.

questions.q: The Human Development Index is computed from which three dimensions?
options: Longevity, access to knowledge and standard of living
questions.explanation: HDI uses life expectancy at birth, access to knowledge (literacy and years of schooling) and a decent standard of living (real per capita income), all scaled between 0 and 1.

questions.q: In the 2019 UNDP ranking of 189 countries, Ethiopia's HDI of 0.485 placed it:
questions.explanation: Ethiopia scored 0.485 and ranked 173 of the 189 countries ranked by UNDP in 2019.

questions.q: Economic growth considers both the quantity and the quality of people's well-being.
questions.explanation: Economic growth is purely quantitative; it is economic development that includes qualitative progress in welfare.

questions.q: Determinist theorists explained the higher development of temperate countries by their location in distinct environments compared with tropical areas.
questions.explanation: Determinists argued temperate regions are more developed than tropical areas because of their distinct cold and hot environments.

questions.q: Which scholar belongs to the geographic determinism school?
questions.explanation: Semple, with Ritter and Huntington, advocated determinism; Febvre and Vidal de la Blache were possibilists.

questions.q: In von Thunen's model, ranching occupies the fourth ring mainly because:
options: livestock can transport themselves to market
questions.explanation: Ranching takes the fourth ring because animals can be self-transporting to the market, unlike bulky or perishable goods.

questions.q: Arrange von Thunen's land-use rings in order starting from the market city.
options: Intensive perishables: vegetables, fruit and dairy
questions.explanation: The correct order is perishables (dairy), forest products, field crops, ranching, then wilderness beyond the fourth ring.

questions.q: Name the German geographer who outlined industrial location theory in his 1909 book 'Theory of the Location of Industries'.
questions.explanation: Alfred Weber, a Heidelberg economics professor, presented the least-cost location model in 1909.

questions.q: In Weber's model, which of the three key factors comes first in fixing the firm's location, with the other two used only for adjustment?
questions.explanation: Weber first determined the least transport-cost location and then adjusted it for labor costs and agglomeration economies, making transport the primary factor.

questions.q: A firm computes a material index of 0.4. According to Weber it should locate:
options: at the mouth of a mine
questions.explanation: An index below 1 means the product outweighs the used inputs, so the firm should locate nearer to the market.

questions.q: Under Christaller's marketing principle, list the successive numbers of centers served starting from 1, and say what this achieves.
questions.answer: 1, 3, 9, 27|serves many consumers from a few centers
questions.explanation: The K = 3 rule follows 1, 3, 9, 27 ..., so several consumers are served from a small number of service centers.

g11-geography-ug5-t2.overview: Climate extremes such as droughts, floods, heat waves and plagues strike hardest where incomes are lowest, turning temporary shocks into lasting poverty. This lesson links warming trends to livelihood losses, flood damage in Ethiopia, poverty traps and the geography of risk up to the 2030s.
objectives: Define climate extremes and give examples of extreme temperature and rainfall events
Describe recent human-induced warming and its projected levels for 2040 and 2100
Explain how climate extremes deepen poverty through assets, health, education and infrastructure
Evaluate how flooding harms farming households using the Itang District case from Gambella
Describe poverty traps, critical thresholds and the geography of climate-related poverty risk
g11-geography-ug5-t2.simple: Climate extremes are excessive values of weather elements, such as temperature, rainfall, droughts, floods, hail storms and heat waves, above or below normal thresholds over an area and time. Human-induced warming reached about 1.0 degree C above pre-industrial levels in 2017 and could reach 1.5 degree C by 2040. Droughts, floods and plagues cut crop yields, kill livestock, damage infrastructure and force poor families to consume or sell their assets. Around 10 percent of the world lives on 1.90 USD a day and about 850 million people survive on less than 1.25 USD, mostly in sub-Saharan Africa. Repeated shocks can push households into poverty traps from which they cannot escape, as the cases of the Itang District in Ethiopia and a retired soldier in Burkina Faso show.
g11-geography-ug5-t2.detailed:
What climate extremes are. Climate extremes are excess temperature and rainfall events, and the environmental hazards that follow them, triggered by recurrent climate change over longer periods. Human-induced warming had already reached about 1.0 degree C above pre-industrial levels by 2017, and is projected to reach 1.5 degree C by 2040 and 1.75 degree C by the turn of the 21st century if the current trend continues. Curiously, the warming has been larger in diurnal minimum temperatures than in maxima. Rainfall has increased in the middle and high latitudes but shown decreasing trends in the tropical and sub-tropical areas over the same period, which is why heat waves, cold waves, floods and droughts keep expanding over wider arid and semi-arid areas.

How extremes erode livelihoods. Extreme droughts, floods, landslides, crop failures, livestock deaths, water shortages and plagues interact with human livelihoods by lessening crop yields, increasing pathogens, exacerbating insect attacks and worsening the risk of invasive weeds. The textbook photographs show the face of the problem: livestock dying in the Somali region of Ethiopia in January 2022, a failed sorghum crop in Ethiopia in January 2016, farmers queuing for drinking water in drought-hit Vietnam, and a house flooded by typhoon Goni in the Philippines in 2020. Such events damage the asset bases of water, livestock and crops as well as people's access to finance, health and education.

Poverty among the exposed. Extremely poor people receive only 1.90 United States Dollars a day, and about 10 percent of the global population lives at or below this line. An estimated 850 million people live on less than 1.25 USD daily, most of them in sub-Saharan Africa. Around 1.3 billion people lack electricity, 900 million lack clean fresh water, 2.6 billion lack improved sanitation, and nearly 800 million rural inhabitants lack all-weather roads. The root causes of climate-related poverty include vulnerability to droughts, flooding, typhoons and locust invasions; weak governance and law enforcement; remoteness from service centers; tenure insecurity; inadequate infrastructure; poor market access and weak social networks; household size, age and dependency structures; unemployment and underemployment; and shelter and nutrition problems.

Direct and indirect impacts. In the short term, climate extremes directly destroy income, earnings, housing, savings, crops, land and properties, and kill, injure or sicken working people; indirectly they cut labour and output, force consumption of limited assets, relocate government and private spending to emergency response, and disrupt supply chains. In the long term they remove fertile land, raise food prices and debts, reduce food security through malnourishment and stunting, lower educational attainment and life expectancy, cut exports while raising imports, and shrink future resilience. Households led by females, people living in slums and children are the most affected, and poor pastoralists fall into lingering poverty when livestock feed diminishes.

Flooding and the Itang case. Flash floods damage walkways, plantations, infrastructure, stream banks and water and power supplies, causing widespread loss of livelihood assets and displacements. In the Itang District of Ethiopia's Gambella region, households are flooded every year when the Baro River, a tributary of the Nile and the widest river in Ethiopia, overflows; from 2006 to 2012 the area suffered a major flood every year except 2009, when drought struck, with the worst floods in 2007 and 2012 when floodwaters that normally retreat by October were still high in mid-November. Unpredictable flash floods from excessive upland rainfall destroy crops and livestock without warning. Of 431 households surveyed, nearly all reported negative impacts: 94 percent lost crops after the 2007 flood, 51 percent lost livestock, and flooded grazing land halved dairy production in 2007, while destroyed crops raised staple food prices. People cope through short-term measures (moving property and livestock to relatives, selling animals early, harvesting premature crops), long-term measures (digging ditches, raising house floors, erecting boundary walls) and, after floods, appeals to social networks plus government and NGO help, but repeated floods erode this social capital, so prevention is not enough as floods grow harsher.

Poverty traps and thresholds. Poverty traps form when extreme climates repeatedly damage poor people and the impacts persist for years or decades. People exposed to recurring droughts, floods and famines consume or sell assets during disasters and sickness, which deters the building of human capital and weakens the capacity to adapt and cope with the next shock. A critical threshold arises when non-climate variables compound: when social-network ties repeatedly break, reciprocal support weakens, and the coping capacity of the already poor collapses into aggravated, lingering poverty. The textbook's second case study shows this vividly: Ag Ayad, a 1937-born Burkina Faso army veteran, held 135 cattle, 87 sheep and 45 goats before the 1973-74 drought took 75 cattle and forced him to sell 30, his brothers lost everything and joined his household, and after the 2004 drought and locust invasion, the loss of 165 small ruminants in a sudden flood of the Beli River in 2011, and a bird invasion that wiped out his 2012 millet harvest, he had to sell even a handcart to buy food - his small gardening profits could not rebuild the herd.

The geography of the risk. Extreme poverty concentrates in sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia and Southeast Asia. North Africa, South Africa and the Mediterranean region face rising temperatures with decreasing rainfall, while South and East Asia see rising rainfall; many of these regions combine high poverty with large climatic shifts, and the tropics, experiencing the largest comparative climate changes, are identified as climate change 'hot-spots'. Recent studies warn that without vigorous action, nearly 325 million extremely poor people may live in 49 countries highly vulnerable to natural hazards - mainly in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia - during the 2030s. Eleven countries most at risk of disaster-induced poverty are Bangladesh, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Ethiopia, Kenya, Madagascar, Nepal, Nigeria, Pakistan, South Sudan, Sudan and Uganda; other threatened states include Benin, the Central African Republic, Chad, Gambia, Guinea Bissau, Haiti, Liberia, Mali, North Korea, Zimbabwe, Niger, Somalia, Yemen, Afghanistan, Cameroon, Myanmar and Papua New Guinea. Disaster risk control should therefore be a basic element of poverty reduction, caring for livelihoods as well as lives, and future development goals must embrace disaster and climate targets.

keyTerms.def: Excessive values of climatic (weather) elements above or below the normal thresholds over a specific geographic area and time, such as severe droughts, floods, hail storms, heat waves and tornadoes; rare but disastrous.
Living on about 1.90 USD per day (the extreme poor) or below 1.25 USD per day; roughly 10 percent of humanity and 850 million people respectively, with the majority in sub-Saharan Africa.
An endless vicious cycle in which repeated climate shocks destroy assets and coping capacity, so people lack the resources needed to escape poverty.
The degree to which poor people and places are exposed to harm from droughts, floods, typhoons and locust invasions because of poverty, marginal locations and weak services.
A household that combines crop cultivation with livestock raising for subsistence, the livelihood type dominating the Itang District of Gambella.
A sudden, unpredictable flood from excessive rainfall in upland mountain regions that can destroy crops and livestock without warning.
The reciprocal support, shelter, food and financial help people draw from ties with relatives and neighbors; repeated floods erode it.
The turning point at which accumulated harm becomes irremediable, such as when repeatedly broken network ties leave the poor without reciprocal support.

workedExamples.problem: In the Itang survey after the 2007 flood, 94 percent of 431 households reported severely damaged or destroyed crops, and 51 percent reported livestock losses. Compute the approximate number of households reporting each loss.
workedExamples.given: Total households surveyed = 431; crop losses = 94 percent; livestock losses = 51 percent.
workedExamples.formula: Number of households = percent of households x total households
workedExamples.answer: About 405 households lost crops and about 220 lost livestock, showing how one flood year stripped nearly the whole community of its harvest and many of its animals.

workedExamples.problem: Check the arithmetic of the Burkina Faso case study: starting from 135 cattle, the veteran lost 75 in the 1973-74 drought and sold 30 more to save the rest. How many remained, and does it agree with his later report?
workedExamples.given: Initial herd = 135 cattle; lost in drought = 75; sold = 30.
workedExamples.formula: Remaining cattle = initial herd - losses - sales
workedExamples.answer: He had exactly 30 cattle left, which matches his statement that in 2004 he lost 20 of the 30 heads he then owned - the numbers in the case study are internally consistent.

workedExamples.problem: Using the IPCC-style projections in the lesson, compute the additional warming expected between 2017 and 2040, and between 2040 and 2100.
workedExamples.given: Warming of 1.0 degree C already reached in 2017; projection of 1.5 degree C by 2040 and 1.75 degree C at the end of the 21st century.
workedExamples.formula: Additional warming = later level - earlier level
workedExamples.calculation: Additional warming = 0.5 degree C and then 0.25 degree C
workedExamples.answer: A further 0.5 degree C is expected by 2040 and another 0.25 degree C by about 2100, meaning most of the projected century increase arrives in the next two decades, when today's poor are still paying for yesterday's shocks.

commonMistakes: Treating climate extremes as everyday weather, when they are rare events with disastrous impacts on life and biodiversity.
Reversing the rainfall trends, claiming the tropics are getting wetter when the textbook reports increasing rain in middle and high latitudes but decreasing rain in tropical and sub-tropical areas.
Mixing up the 1.90 USD and 1.25 USD poverty lines when quoting the shares of the world's poor.
Thinking a single disaster creates a poverty trap, when traps need repeated, lasting shocks over years or decades.
Counting only direct short-term losses and ignoring indirect, long-term impacts such as rising food prices, growing debt and falling school attainment.
Believing preventive measures like ditches and raised floors are always sufficient, when the Itang study shows they work only for minor floods.
Forgetting that coping through social networks is itself eroded by repeated floods, so it cannot be relied on forever.
applications: Linking the recurrent droughts of Ethiopia's Somali region and other lowlands to livestock death, asset loss and deepening pastoral poverty.
Explaining why annual Baro River floods in Itang District, Gambella, demand better embankments, early warnings and protected grazing land.
Planning rural roads for Ethiopia's countryside, remembering that nearly 800 million rural people worldwide lack all-weather roads and therefore markets, clinics and schools.
Showing how the 1973-74 Sahel drought proves that climate policy must double as poverty policy through livestock insurance and fodder banks.
Preparing for the projected 325 million extremely poor people in 49 highly vulnerable countries in the 2030s, with Ethiopia named among the eleven most exposed states.
Using the short-term and long-term impact table to design post-disaster responses that protect crop and livestock assets, school attendance and health care.
g11-geography-ug5-t2.summary: Climate extremes are rare but disastrous deviations of temperature and rainfall from normal thresholds that hit poorest where incomes are lowest, with warming already about 1.0 degree C above pre-industrial levels in 2017. Extremes strip households of crops, livestock, roads, schooling and health care, and repeated shocks that erode assets and social networks produce poverty traps. Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia carry the greatest risk, with up to 325 million extremely poor people and 49 highly vulnerable countries projected for the 2030s, Ethiopia among them.

config.title: Responding to Floods in Itang District

steps.label: Before the flood
steps.detail: Move household property and livestock to relatives in safer areas, sell animals early, and harvest premature crops.

steps.label: Prepare long term
steps.detail: Dig ditches around property and farms, raise the floors of homes, and erect boundary walls.

steps.label: After the flood
steps.detail: Appeal to social networks for shelter, food, money and materials; accept government and NGO assistance.

steps.label: Last resort
steps.detail: Sell livestock and property to pay for food and other necessities.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Prevention works only for minor floods, so better infrastructure and warnings are needed as floods grow harsher.

questions.q: Climate extremes are best defined as:
options: Weather elements taking excessive values above or below normal thresholds over an area and time
Slow climate change measured over a century
questions.explanation: The textbook defines extreme climate as an excessive value of climatic elements below or above the normal thresholds in a specific area and time, and such extremes are rare but disastrous.

questions.q: The daily income that marks people as extremely poor is about:
questions.explanation: Extremely poor people receive only 1.90 USD per day, and about 10 percent of the global population lives within this threshold.

questions.q: Human-induced warming reached about 1.0 degree C above pre-industrial levels by 2017.
questions.explanation: The textbook states human-induced warming reached about 1.0 degree C above pre-industrial levels in 2017, with 1.5 degree C projected by 2040.

questions.q: Rainfall in tropical and sub-tropical areas has shown increasing trends over the period of study.
questions.explanation: Rainfall has decreased in tropical and sub-tropical areas, while increasing in the middle and high latitudes.

questions.q: Between 2006 and 2012 the Itang District of Gambella suffered a major flood every year apart from:
questions.explanation: The area suffered a major flood every year from 2006 to 2012 except 2009, when drought struck; 2007 and 2012 were the worst years.

questions.q: Name the river whose annual overflow floods the households of Itang District, Gambella.
questions.explanation: Households are flooded annually when the Baro River, a tributary of the Nile and the widest river in Ethiopia, overflows.

questions.q: Explain why relying on social networks to cope with floods proved unsustainable in Itang.
questions.answer: repeated floods erode social capital|repeated demand weakens reciprocal support

g11-geography-ug5-t3.overview: Landlocked countries possess no seacoast and must cross at least one neighboring state to take part in world trade. This lesson shows how that position raises transport costs, multiplies transit charges and delays, and exposes trade to political disputes, with Ethiopia as the central example.
objectives: Describe the characteristic features of landlocked countries
Explain how the lack of sea access raises transport costs and lowers trade competitiveness
Assess the dependence of landlocked states on the infrastructure of transit neighbors
Identify the political and conflict-related barriers that disrupt landlocked trade
Evaluate Ethiopia's port dependence and its possible alternative corridors
g11-geography-ug5-t3.simple: Landlocked countries are states without any seacoast: rivers and lakes may exist inside their borders, but every boundary is land based. There are 49 such countries, about one fifth (20 percent) of the world's nations, dispersed across all continents and clustered in the mid-regions of continents. To import and export they depend on transit neighbors' roads, railways and ports, so transport costs rise, exports lose competitiveness and imports become expensive. Doubling transport costs can cut trade volume by about 80 percent, and doubling travel costs can cut tourism demand as much as eightfold. Transit fees, licensing, customs hurdles, border delays and political conflicts add further burdens. Ethiopia lost the use of the ports of Assab and Massawa after 1997 amid conflict with Eritrea and now relies mainly on the port of Djibouti.
g11-geography-ug5-t3.detailed:
What landlocked means. Landlocked countries are those that do not possess any seacoast. Rivers may run through part of the territory and lakes or other bodies of water may lie inside the borders, yet every border is land based rather than an ocean shore. They occupy the mid-regions of continents, are geographically dispersed across all continents, and constitute about one fifth of the world's nations. Many were created by three historical events: the end of the First World War, the end of colonization, and the collapse and splitting of the former Soviet Union. In Africa, colonial powers drew borders that left some states completely enclosed by others, and most African states have retained these colonial border lines.

The price of distance from the sea. Landlocked countries lie far from seaports and incur higher transport costs in foreign trade, and the cost of international transport services is a crucial determinant of a country's trade competitiveness. Higher trade costs reduce national welfare and inhibit growth by making imports expensive and exports non-competitive. Doubling transport costs reduces a country's trade volume by around 80 percent, and excessive transport costs also block trade in services: doubling travel cost reduces the demand for tourism as much as eightfold. Landlocked states therefore suffer noticeable drawbacks when they compete in global markets against coastal economies.

Hostage to the neighbor's infrastructure. Landlocked countries are entirely dependent on the infrastructure of their transit neighbors for access to international markets. If only routes of poor quality are available, the cost of overland trade is significantly higher than it would otherwise be, so landlocked trade costs reflect the level of development of the transit neighbors. The problem is most severe in western and central Africa. Burundi, despite better domestic roads, is hamstrung by its neighbors' poor transit network, and its short direct passage to the sea, the Central Corridor over Tanzania to Dar es Salaam, suffers from a very poor transit setup across that route. In the case of the Central African Republic, the derelict corridor country has no reliable all-weather road network to the sea; its transit through Cameroon is impenetrable during the rainy season, and its transit corridor along the Oubangui River over the neighboring state is closed in the dry season because of diminished water flow and security reasons.

Charges and paperwork. Transiting a country involves a host of transit and custom charges, some paid upfront and some during the journey, often demanded in hard currency when local currency cannot be converted. The charges include transit goods licenses, border fees, temporary road licenses, foreign vehicle permits, toll charges, foreign commercial licenses, customs verification of containers, posting and cancellation of security bonds, and police escorts and convoy costs; agency fees at ports may even exceed domestic freight charges. Some regions now lighten the load: common warrants announced in the Southern African Development Community (SADC) and the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA) let road freight travel within member countries without local permits or licenses, and Bhutan handles its transit trade through its own customs, never touched by Indian officials.

Politics and conflict. Political issues rank next to transport as challenges. Landlocked states usually hold little negotiating power over their transit neighbors, lack access rights during conflicts, and may see trade routes cut by border closures even when bilateral relations are good. Bolivia faces severe transit limitations in Chile after more than 100 years of weak relations; Armenia has been blocked by Turkey and Azerbaijan; and the conflict between Ethiopia and Eritrea denied Ethiopia the use of the ports of Assab and Massawa after 1997. Ethiopia now routes its transit trade through Djibouti, but that single corridor never satisfies its wide demand because the transport network is poorly developed, and alternative routes through Kenya, Sudan and Somalia are also weakly developed. Recent promising developments between Ethiopia and Eritrea may again open the two Red Sea ports in the future.

Delays everywhere. Mean transit delays during border crossings across Africa range from 24 to 48 hours and can stretch into weeks. The mean trip from Kampala (Uganda) to Mombasa (Kenya) takes about 21 days and can take even 60 days, and similar delays repeat in other transit and port areas. Overall, landlocked countries face dependence on the infrastructure levels of transit nations, fees and direct costs from administrative burdens, and time delays in their export trades, which together explain their weak and underachieving economic performance compared with coastal states.

keyTerms.def: A state that possesses no seacoast; every border is land based, although rivers and inland water bodies may lie within its territory.
A country a landlocked state must cross by road, rail, river or other route to reach a seaport and international markets.
The ability of a country's goods to compete in world markets; it falls steeply when transport costs are high.
Fees collected while crossing another country, including transit good licenses, border fees, temporary road licenses, foreign vehicle permits, tolls and security bonds.
A widely accepted foreign currency in which transit payments are often demanded, though landlocked traders may lack the means to convert local currency.
The shutting of crossing points, usually during conflicts or political crises, which cuts trade routes of landlocked states.
An agreement in SADC and COMESA allowing road freight to move within member countries without local permits or licenses.
Burundi's short direct passage to the sea over Tanzania to the port of Dar es Salaam, burdened by a poor transit setup.

workedExamples.problem: A landlocked country exports goods worth 2 billion USD a year. If its transport costs double, apply the textbook rule to estimate the remaining trade volume.
workedExamples.given: Initial trade volume = 2,000 million USD; doubling of transport costs cuts trade volume by about 80 percent.
workedExamples.formula: Rejected trade = initial trade volume x 0.80; remaining = initial trade volume - rejected trade
workedExamples.answer: Only about 400 million USD of trade survives the doubling of transport costs - the reduction is a full 80 percent, which is why high freight costs strangle landlocked exporters.

workedExamples.problem: A landlocked country receives 16,000 tourist arrivals a year. Estimate arrivals if travel costs to the country double.
workedExamples.given: Current arrivals = 16,000; doubling travel cost reduces tourism demand as much as eightfold.
workedExamples.formula: New demand = original demand / eightfold reduction
workedExamples.answer: Arrivals fall to about 2,000, showing that distance and transport costs suffocate the export of tourism services as surely as they do goods trade.

workedExamples.problem: A freight planner schedules the Kampala to Mombasa trip in 5 days, but the mean African transit reality is about 21 days and can reach 60 days. Compute the extra days in the mean and in the worst recorded case.
workedExamples.given: Planned trip = 5 days; mean actual trip = 21 days; extreme case = 60 days.
workedExamples.formula: Extra days = actual days - planned days
workedExamples.answer: On average 16 extra days are lost, and up to 55 in bad years, consistent with African border-crossing delays of 24 to 48 hours at every boundary.

workedExamples.problem: Which of Ethiopia's neighboring corridors - Djibouti, or routes through Kenya, Sudan and Somalia - offer a well-developed transport network, and what follows for Ethiopia's trade?
workedExamples.given: The Djibouti corridor serves Ethiopia's transit trade but never satisfies the demand; alternatives through Kenya, Sudan and Somalia are poorly developed.
workedExamples.formula: Assessment rule: match each corridor's network quality against the country's transport demand
workedExamples.substitution: Djibouti route: used, congested demand. Kenyan, Sudanese and Somali routes: poorly developed networks.
workedExamples.calculation: No corridor meets the full demand, so capacity depends on one country's single port.
workedExamples.answer: None is fully adequate; Ethiopia depends on one congested corridor, so its trade needs corridor investment and diversified access such as the possible reopening of Assab and Massawa.

commonMistakes: Believing rivers, lakes or borders along a lake make a country non-landlocked; only an ocean coast counts.
Assuming landlocked countries are rare or found only in Africa, when 49 exist - one fifth of all states - on every continent.
Remembering only that exports suffer, when high transport costs also make imports expensive and shrink national welfare.
Ignoring that the transit neighbor's infrastructure level directly sets the landlocked country's trade cost.
Blaming geography alone for Ethiopia's port loss, when the 1998 conflict with Eritrea closed the ports of Assab and Massawa.
Treating administrative hurdles as trivial, when agency fees, bonds and escorts can even exceed domestic freight costs.
Forgetting that weak negotiating power leaves most landlocked states with little leverage over transit neighbors.
applications: Explaining Ethiopia's shift from the ports of Assab and Massawa to the port of Djibouti after 1997, and what that shift costs shippers and consumers.
Arguing for expanding the Djibouti corridor's rail and road capacity because the existing route never satisfies the demand.
Comparing Ethiopia's situation with Burundi's Central Corridor over Tanzania and the counry that transits by the Oubangui River, to see which geography is hardest.
Using the 24 to 48 hour border delay figure to press for harmonized customs procedures under COMESA and SADC common warrants.
Debating how the recent improvement in Ethiopia and Eritrea relations could reopen Assab and Massawa and lower import prices.
Applying the trade-cost rule to a hypothetical doubling of freight rates between Addis Ababa and Djibouti to dramatize why logistics dominate policy.
g11-geography-ug5-t3.summary: Landlocked countries - 49 states, or about one fifth of the world's nations, most located in mid-continental positions - pay the highest transport penalty in development because every consignment must cross a transit neighbor. Doubling transport costs can erase about 80 percent of trade volume and eightfold-fall tourism demand, while infrastructure weakness, transit charges, conflicts and weak negotiating power stretch any trip into weeks, as on the Kampala to Mombasa route. Ethiopia's post-1997 reliance on Djibouti illustrates both the burden and the importance of good transit agreements.

g11-geography-ug5-t4.overview: Africa feeds itself largely through trade among its own regions, yet formal flows stay small and informal trade thrives. This lesson maps the trends, the leading exporters and importers, the commodity mix and the tariff and non-tariff barriers that shape Ethiopia's position in intra-African commerce.
objectives: Describe the flow trends of agricultural trade within Africa since 2000
Identify the top exporters and importers of intra-African trade using export and import shares
Interpret the commodity composition of food and agricultural trade flows in Africa
Explain how tariffs, non-tariff measures and informal currency exchange distort trade
Evaluate Ethiopia's position, partners and challenges in intra-African trade
g11-geography-ug5-t4.simple: Population growth, rising incomes and urbanization keep lifting Africa's demand for local food markets. Regional Economic Communities build preferential tariffs, free trade zones and customs unions: AMU has 5 members, COMESA 19, ECOWAS 15 and SADC 16. Intra-African agricultural trade rose steadily from about 2007, peaked in 2013, dipped, then resumed growth in 2016, led by SADC and COMESA exporters. South Africa dominates formal trade, exporting nearly a third of intra-African exports, while Kenya and Egypt are leading importers; Ethiopia's export share fell from 2.8 to 0.5 percent. Only 6 of the top 20 exported products - maize, wheat, rice, cattle, apples and vegetables - directly serve food security, and tariffs, non-tariff measures, weak infrastructure and black-market exchange rates push time-sensitive goods into informal trade.
g11-geography-ug5-t4.detailed:
Rising demand, lopsided trade. Population growth coupled with rising income and urbanization is driving growing demand for local food markets across Africa, creating opportunities for intraregional trade expansion and challenges for national food security. Present-day Africa's world trade is dominated by imports of processed food products and by exports of untreated, unprocessed nonfood products, a pattern common in many countries, and it remains pertinent to ask whether current supply capabilities can meet the emerging needs.

Regional Economic Communities. Africa's agricultural exports have increased since 2000 in the form of intra-African trade, although participation in world trade remains low. Regional Economic Communities (RECs) have established preferential tariff agreements, free trade zones and customs unions among neighboring members: the Arab Maghreb Union (AMU) with 5 member states, COMESA with 19, the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) with 15 and SADC with 16.

Trends and retention shares. The USD value of intra-African food and agricultural trade rose steadily from roughly 2007, peaked in 2013, declined significantly, then resumed a general upward trend in 2016. Intra-continental exports grew faster annually than extra-continental and global exports from 2008 to 2015, while the reverse held in later years. Retention differs sharply by region: in 2016-2018 SADC retained 84 percent of its intra-African exports, ECOWAS 79 percent, COMESA 66 percent and AMU 60 percent, whereas ECCAS shipped the largest share of its exports outside its region, keeping only 46 percent within the REC, down from 58 percent in 2005-2007 - although ECCAS' total exports are small. ECOWAS saw the sharpest intra-REC export spike in 2013, and only SADC shows an obvious increase in exports since 2016.

Top exporters and importers. The top 10 intra-African exporters account for roughly 70 percent of the formal market, while agricultural imports are more widely dispersed, with the top importers holding only about half. South Africa remained the dominant player across 2005-2007 and 2016-2018: it exported nearly a third of all intra-African formal exports (29.8 percent, then 32.2 percent) and imported roughly a tenth (11.5 percent, then 8.3 percent), with its export share rising while its import share fell. Export shares increased for Egypt (8.7 percent), Uganda (6.4 percent), Kenya (6.2 percent) and Tanzania, while they declined for Cote d'Ivoire, Zambia, Namibia, Tunisia and Ethiopia, whose share sank from 2.8 to 0.5 percent. Among importers, Kenya, Egypt, Zimbabwe, Mozambique and the DRC increased their shares while Namibia, Botswana, Libya and Nigeria decreased theirs. South Africa, Kenya, Namibia and Egypt are simultaneously top exporters and large importers, jointly holding 25 percent of intra-continental agricultural imports, and Eastern, Southern African and Maghreb countries lead the trade, with other western and central African countries playing only a small role.

Ethiopia's position. Ethiopia's top 10 import sources account for 99 percent of its intra-African imports - the main sources being Morocco, South Africa and Egypt - and its top 10 export destinations take 98 percent of its intra-African exports, above all Somalia, Djibouti and Kenya. At the same time the textbook shows Ethiopia's formal export share of intra-African trade shrinking from 2.8 percent in 2005-2007 to 0.5 percent in 2016-2018, a warning about lost competitiveness within the continent.

What is actually traded. Africa's intra-continental agricultural trade is more diversified than South Asia's intraregional trade but less diversified than Europe's. Among the top 20 products exported within Africa, only 6 - maize, wheat, rice, cattle, apples and vegetables - play a key food security and nutritional role for African consumers. The remainder consists of sweeteners and fats, beverages and processed foods, and traditional exports such as tea, coffee, palm oil, cotton and tobacco products.

Barriers and the informal escape. Tariff and non-tariff barriers are the main challenges hindering formal intra-African trade, and in many cases non-tariff measures are more trade-restrictive than tariffs. Both tariffs and non-tariff measures can incentivize trans-shipment and smuggling and raise risks for businesses trying to build streamlined, secure and transparent supply chains. Administrative barriers cause undue time delays that are unworkable for products that deteriorate without cold storage and transport, which partly explains the high reliance on informal trade of fruits, vegetables and other time-sensitive goods, and such delays and burdens also discourage private investment in regional supply chains. Ethiopia's East African border trade shows the currency problem: agreed prices are converted into Birr at black-market rates - Birr 1 officially equals about 13 Kenyan Shillings, but only 5-6 on the black market, while the Djibouti franc's black-market rate hovered around 30 percent of official value - so purchasing power of the Birr falls, terms of trade turn unfavorable to Ethiopia, and informal export values drop far below imports, mirroring the national trade deficit. Tapping Africa's regional trade potential therefore requires coordination between regions, strong production and processing capacity, and investment in roads, transport and information systems along key corridors, with market information for priority agri-food value chains; if barriers fall, time-sensitive agri-foods could flourish regionally, nutrition-sensitive demand permitting.

keyTerms.def: A regional bloc such as AMU, COMESA, ECOWAS or SADC that builds preferential tariffs, free trade zones or customs unions among neighboring members.
Trade in goods, here food and agricultural products, exchanged between African countries rather than with the rest of the world.
Registered, documented trade that passes customs and contributes to official statistics; the top ten exporters supply about 70 percent of formal intra-African food exports.
Undocumented trade in items like fruits and vegetables that bypasses official channels, often driven by long delays and currency problems.
A trade restriction other than a tariff, such as licensing, inspection or customs delays; in many cases more trade-restrictive than tariffs themselves.
An arrangement in which members reduce or remove tariffs among themselves, one of the instruments RECs use to promote integration.
The ratio between export and import prices; the black-market depreciation of the Birr made Ethiopia's terms of trade unfavorable in informal trade.
A broker in Ethiopian informal markets who negotiates prices and converts currencies, typically carrying a small calculator.

workedExamples.problem: In 2016-2018 the top 10 intra-African exporters held 71 percent of formal export trade, with South Africa alone on 32.2 percent. Compute the share left for all remaining African exporters.
workedExamples.given: Top 10 exporters' share = 71 percent; South Africa's share = 32.2 percent.
workedExamples.answer: All countries outside the top 10 share only 29 percent of formal agricultural exports, confirming how concentrated intra-African trade is on South Africa and nine others.

workedExamples.problem: Compute the share of formal intra-African agricultural imports held by countries outside the top importing group in 2016-2018.
workedExamples.given: Top importers' combined share = about 50.2 percent (roughly half of formal trade).
workedExamples.formula: Remaining share = 100 percent - top importers' share
workedExamples.answer: About 49.8 percent of imports fall to the many countries outside the top group, showing imports are far more widely dispersed than exports.

workedExamples.problem: A border trader changes Birr into Kenyan Shillings. The official rate is Birr 1 = Ksh 13 while the black market gives Birr 1 = Ksh 5.5. By what percentage does the black-market value fall short of the official rate?
workedExamples.given: Official rate = 13 Ksh per Birr; black-market rate = 5.5 Ksh per Birr (within the observed 5-6 range).
workedExamples.formula: Shortfall = (official rate - black-market rate) / official rate x 100
workedExamples.answer: The Birr loses about 58 percent of its official value in informal exchange, which is exactly why the case study reports unfavorable terms of trade and a trade deficit for Ethiopia.

workedExamples.problem: Rank the top intra-African exporters of 2016-2018 from these shared percentages: Egypt 8.7, Uganda 6.4, Kenya 6.2, Cote d'Ivoire 4.6, South Africa 32.2.
workedExamples.given: Export shares: South Africa 32.2, Egypt 8.7, Uganda 6.4, Kenya 6.2, Cote d'Ivoire 4.6.
workedExamples.formula: Ranking rule: order countries from largest to smallest export share
workedExamples.calculation: Ranks 1 to 5 assigned by descending share
workedExamples.answer: South Africa (1), Egypt (2), Uganda (3), Kenya (4), Cote d'Ivoire (5) - matching Table 5.2 of the textbook.

commonMistakes: Reversing the trade pattern, when Africa exports unprocessed nonfood and agricultural products and imports processed food products.
Forgetting that non-tariff measures are often more trade-restrictive than tariffs themselves.
Assuming all RECs keep their exports within the bloc, when retention ranges from 84 percent in SADC down to 46 percent in ECCAS.
Misplacing Cote d'Ivoire, the sole top exporter from ECOWAS, among southern African SADC countries.
Confusing import-share trends, since Nigeria and Libya lost import share while Mozambique and the DRC gained.
Overlooking informal trade and black-market currency gaps, which depress the value of Ethiopian cross-border exports.
Reading the 2013 peak as continuous growth, when the trade value declined significantly before resuming its rise in 2016.
applications: Interpreting Ethiopia's fall from 2.8 to 0.5 percent of intra-African export share between 2005-2007 and 2016-2018 as a lost-competitiveness alert.
Mapping Ethiopia's top export destinations - Somalia, Djibouti and Kenya - to target border and corridor trade promotion.
Explaining why fruits and vegetables cross borders informally when customs delays would ruin them without cold storage.
Tracing how the gap between the official and black-market Birr rate gives Ethiopian traders unfavorable terms of trade and a deficit in the informal balance.
Arguing for cold chains, corridor roads and market information systems to unlock time-sensitive agri-food value chains in East Africa.
Using the REC membership numbers to plan which bloc Ethiopia should prioritize for tariff-free market access.
g11-geography-ug5-t4.summary: Intra-African agricultural trade has grown since 2000 - rising from about 2007, peaking in 2013 and resuming in 2016 - and is led by SADC and COMESA members, yet it remains modest in world trade. South Africa alone exports about a third of formal intra-African exports while Ethiopia's share fell to 0.5 percent; only 6 of the top 20 traded products directly serve food security. Tariff and non-tariff barriers, weak infrastructure and black-market exchange rates keep formal flows small and push time-sensitive goods into informal trade, so integration needs corridor investment, coordination and smooth procedures.
